title: Workflow, agent and augmented LLM patterns for Claude

units.text: Select appropriate architectural patterns
What you will be able to do
Describe the augmented LLM and explain why every workflow and agent pattern is built from it
Tell a workflow from an agent by asking who decides the next step, and weigh what each choice costs
Justify starting with a single optimized call and adding complexity only when it measurably falls short
Pick the right workflow for a task: prompt chaining, routing, parallelization (sectioning or voting) or orchestrator-workers
Recognise when an evaluator-optimizer loop fits and when a programmatic check is the better tool
Key concept
Who controls the next step

Every pattern in this lesson is made of augmented LLM calls. What separates them is whether your code fixes the path those calls take (a workflow) or the model chooses its next action at run time (an agent).

The augmented LLM as the building block
Every architecture in this lesson, from a two-step pipeline to an autonomous coding agent, is made from one unit: the
augmented LLM

. This is a model call extended with retrieval, tools and memory. Claude does not just receive these capabilities passively. It writes its own search queries, chooses which tool to call, and decides what information to keep. A pattern describes how several of these units are wired together. It never replaces the unit.

In practice a single call carries more than the user's text. Claude receives the prompt along with the system prompt, the tool definitions and the conversation history, and it may answer in text, request tool calls, or do both. So even before you choose a pattern, one call can search, look things up and act.

Two parts of the implementation matter most. First, the capabilities should fit your use case: a support assistant needs order lookup, not a general web crawler. Second, each capability needs a clear, well-documented interface the model can understand. The Model Context Protocol is one way to connect third-party tools through a simple client; choosing among integration mechanisms is covered in
connection protocols
. Once each call has the right augmentations, the architectural question becomes how those calls are arranged.
Checkpoint 1 of 9
Check yourself
A team is building an internal assistant that answers employees' questions about HR policy. Before choosing any workflow or agent pattern, how should they set up the single model call?
Skip augmentations for now and choose an agent pattern, because the pattern provides retrieval and tools
Give the call a policy-document retrieval tool with a clear, well-documented interface that the model can query itself
Run the document search in their own code and paste the results into the prompt, because the model cannot write its own search queries
Connect every tool they have, such as a web crawler, code execution and the CRM, so the call can handle any question that comes up

Workflows versus agents: who decides the next step
Predict first
A system calls Claude three times, and each call can use a search tool. What makes it an agent rather than a workflow?
Claude decides at run time what to do next and when it is finished
It makes more than one LLM call per request
Claude has access to tools
Workflows and agents are both agentic systems, and they differ in one thing: who controls the sequence. In a
workflow
, your code decides the order of calls: classify, then draft, then translate. In an
agent
, the model directs its own process and tool use. Using tools, or making many calls, does not by itself make something an agent.

The agent's mechanics are simple. It is a model using tools in a loop and acting on what comes back. The Claude Agent SDK runs this cycle: Claude evaluates the current state and requests tool calls, the SDK runs them, and each set of results goes back to Claude for its next decision. The loop stops when Claude gives a response with no tool calls. In a bug-fix run, Claude might run the tests, read the failing files, edit one, and run the tests again before it reports that all three pass. Because the model judges its progress from these real results, agents usually also get
stopping conditions
, such as a maximum number of iterations, so they stay under control.

Agents fit open-ended problems where you cannot predict how many steps are needed or hardcode a path, such as resolving a SWE-bench task that touches many files. That autonomy has a price: higher cost and the risk of compounding errors, where one bad decision feeds the next. Agents call for extensive testing in sandboxed environments, guardrails, and enough trust in the model's decision-making to let it run for many turns.

Checkpoint 2 of 9
Check yourself
Every incoming invoice goes through the same three steps: extract the fields, check them against the purchase order with a lookup tool, then draft an approval email. Which design fits best, and why?
A workflow, because it makes only three LLM calls, and systems with more calls than that have to be agents
A workflow in which code fixes the order extract → check → draft, because the steps are known in advance and the path stays predictable
An agent, because the steps use a tool, and tool use is what makes the model decide the order at run time
An agent with a maximum-iteration stopping condition, because the cap makes it as predictable as a workflow
Sources
Start simple and add complexity only when it pays

The default is the simplest design that works, and that is often not an agentic system at all. For many applications, a single LLM call improved with retrieval and in-context examples is enough. Current Claude models handle most multistep reasoning inside one call, so a pipeline you build to imitate that reasoning may add nothing.

Every layer you add costs something. Agentic systems usually trade latency and cost for better task performance, so the real question is whether that gain is worth paying for in this application. Each extra call adds a round trip and more tokens, and each handoff is another place the system can fail. Add a workflow when a single call measurably falls short. Add an agent only when you also need the flexibility of model-driven decisions.

Frameworks deserve the same caution. Tools such as the Claude Agent SDK make it easy to start by handling model calls, tool parsing and chaining. They can also hide the underlying prompts and responses, which makes debugging harder, and they make it tempting to add complexity a simpler setup would not need. Many patterns take only a few lines of code against the API directly. If you do use a framework, understand what it does underneath, because wrong assumptions about it are a common source of errors.
Apply it to your own work
Think of an LLM feature you have seen built as a multi-step pipeline. What measurement would have shown whether one well-prompted call with retrieval was already good enough?
Exam trap
Agents outperform workflows, so a production design should default to an agent.
Why is that wrong?

Prompt chaining and routing: fixed steps and distinct categories

Picking a workflow comes down to a few questions about the task. Are the steps fixed? Do inputs fall into distinct categories? Can the work run in parallel? Can you predict the subtasks before seeing the input? Is there a clear test for quality? Each answer points to a different pattern, and the wrong options in a design review usually answer a question the scenario never asked.
The question each workflow pattern answers
If the task…
Use
Why
Breaks cleanly into fixed sequential subtasks
Prompt chaining
Each call does an easier task; gates check intermediate output
Has distinct input categories that are better handled separately
Routing
Specialized prompts without one input type hurting another
Has independent pieces, or needs several attempts for confidence
Parallelization (sectioning or voting)
Speed, or focused attention per aspect, or diverse outputs
Needs subtasks that depend on the specific input
Orchestrator-workers
A central LLM decides the subtasks at run time
Has clear evaluation criteria and improves with feedback
Evaluator-optimizer
Generate, critique and refine in a loop
Prompt chaining

splits a task into a fixed sequence, and each call processes the output of the one before it. It fits when the task decomposes cleanly into known subtasks. It deliberately trades latency for accuracy, because each call has an easier job. Between steps you can add
gates

, which are programmatic checks that confirm the process is still on track. A gate is ordinary code: a length limit, a schema check, a required field. Writing marketing copy and then translating it is the standard example. A content team that translates copy into three languages and must keep each string within a UI character limit has a fixed sequence plus a deterministic check, so it is a chain with a gate. It does not need another LLM to judge length, and it does not need an orchestrator to decide which languages to produce, because the languages are already known.

Chaining also helps you run the system. Explicit chains are still worth using when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure, because each step is a separate API call you can log, evaluate or branch on. Smaller, consistent subtasks also reduce inconsistency at scale, since each one gets Claude's full attention.
Routing

classifies an input first and then sends it to a specialized follow-up: a different prompt, tool set or process. The reason is separation of concerns. Without routing, tuning one prompt for one kind of input can hurt performance on the others. Routing fits when the categories are distinct and classification is accurate, whether an LLM or a traditional classifier does it. A support queue with billing questions, technical bugs and cancellations, each needing its own tuned prompt, is a routing problem. Running every ticket through all three prompts in a chain wastes calls on the two that don't apply. Running them in parallel and keeping whichever finishes first throws away the reason for having specialists. Routing can also send easy questions to a smaller, cheaper model and hard ones to a more capable model; choosing those models is covered in
model selection
On the exam

Routing is only as good as its categories. If the categories are vague, tickets get misrouted and the specialized prompts never see the inputs they were built for. Before you choose routing, check that the categories are well defined and the classification step is reliable.
Exam trap
Any quality check in a pipeline means an evaluator-optimizer loop.
Why is that wrong?

Checkpoint 5 of 9
Exam question

A content team needs marketing copy generated and then translated into three languages, with a programmatic check confirming each translated string stays within a fixed UI character limit before it is published. Which architectural pattern best fits this requirement?
Prompt chaining, using sequential LLM calls with a programmatic gate that checks translated text length before publishing
Routing, so that each language request is classified and sent to a specialized translation prompt tuned to that locale's conventions
Orchestrator-workers, letting a central LLM decide which languages need translation based on real-time traffic analysis
Evaluator-optimizer, where a second LLM scores each translation and loops until translation quality passes a threshold
Checkpoint 6 of 9
Exam question

A customer support system receives billing questions, technical bugs, and account cancellations. Each category needs a differently tuned prompt, and an initial step must first determine which category a given ticket belongs to before further processing. Which pattern should the team implement?
Parallelization, running the billing, technical, and cancellation prompts simultaneously and merging whichever completes first
Routing, where an initial LLM call classifies the ticket and directs it to the specialized prompt for that category
Prompt chaining, where each ticket is chained through billing, then technical, then cancellation prompts in sequence
Orchestrator-workers, where a central LLM decides at runtime which subtasks the ticket requires and assigns them to worker LLMs

Parallelization and orchestrator-workers: known versus emergent subtasks
Parallelization
runs several LLM calls at the same time and combines their outputs in code. It has two forms. Learn to tell them apart by asking whether the calls do different work or the same work.
Sectioning

splits a task into independent subtasks that run in parallel: one call checks generated code for vulnerabilities while another checks the same code for licensing problems, and code merges both into one report.
Voting
runs the same task several times to get different outputs, for example several prompts reviewing code for vulnerabilities, with the code flagged if any of them finds a problem.

Sectioning often helps quality as well as speed. When a task involves several considerations, LLMs usually do better if each one gets its own call with focused attention. Guardrails are the standard case: one instance answers the user while another screens the query for inappropriate content, which works better than one call doing both. Chaining these checks would be wrong, because neither depends on the other's output. An evaluator-optimizer setup would be wrong too, because neither check is critiquing the other.
Predict first
A pipeline always runs the same five review prompts in parallel on every input. Is that orchestrator-workers?
Orchestrator-workers

looks like parallelization: a central LLM breaks the work down, hands pieces to worker LLMs, and combines their results. The difference is that the subtasks are not fixed in advance. The orchestrator decides them at run time from the specific input. In a coding change, the number of files to edit and what changes in each depend on the request, so nobody can write the fan-out beforehand. A fixed set of five prompts is therefore sectioning. Orchestrator-workers is the wrong choice for simple single-output tasks, when latency is critical, or when the subtasks are predictable enough to define ahead of time. In that last case, use the simpler parallel workflow.
The orchestrator shape: decompose the input at run time, fan out to workers, then synthesize

Exam question

A security team wants one LLM call to check generated code for vulnerabilities while a second, independent LLM call simultaneously checks the same code for licensing issues, with both outputs combined into a single report. Which pattern does this describe?
Parallelization by sectioning, running the vulnerability and licensing checks as independent, simultaneous LLM calls
Parallelization by voting, running the same vulnerability prompt three times and keeping the majority verdict
Evaluator-optimizer, where the licensing checker scores the vulnerability checker's output and requests revisions until both agree
Prompt chaining, where the vulnerability check output is fed into the licensing check as additional context

The evaluator-optimizer loop
In an
evaluator-optimizer

loop, one call produces a response, a second call critiques it against criteria, and the loop repeats until the response passes. It is the same draft, review and revise cycle a human writer goes through. With Claude it is the most common chaining pattern: generate a draft, review it against criteria, then refine based on the review.

The pattern needs two conditions: clear evaluation criteria, and refinement that measurably improves the result. There are two signs it fits. First, the responses clearly get better when a human states their feedback. Second, an LLM can give that feedback itself. Literary translation passes both tests, because an evaluator can spot nuances the first translation missed. Complex search also fits: the evaluator decides whether another round of searching is needed.
Predict first
A generated product title must be valid JSON and no longer than 60 characters. Should a second LLM evaluate it in a loop?
No, because a deterministic programmatic check does this more cheaply and reliably
Yes, but only with voting across three evaluators
Yes, because evaluator-optimizer is the pattern for any quality check

That contrast is the key decision. Use an LLM evaluator when quality is a judgment, such as tone, nuance or completeness, that a model can put into words and the generator can act on. Use a programmatic gate when the test is a rule code can check. Every loop adds at least one more call per round, so stop it with a pass condition rather than letting it run open-ended. Defining the metrics an evaluator scores against is covered in
evaluation metrics
A literary translation loop runs four rounds and the evaluator's score stops rising after round two. What does that tell you about fit?
